extracted.intended_audience: Congressional staff, USPTO policymakers, patent practitioners, industry stakeholders, and IP policy analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate how recent U.S. patent subject matter eligibility jurisprudence (post-Alice) affects innovation, litigation, prosecution, disclosure, trade secrets, national competitiveness, and specific technology sectors (especially life sciences and diagnostics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on startups and small inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: The current judicially created uncertainty resulting from the Supreme Court’s change in subject matter jurisprudence unduly restricts protections especially for small companies, start-ups and single inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters reported that small entities ‘can’t afford to pay the tremendous costs in legal fees and expenses’ and that uncertainty makes it more difficult, and in some cases effectively impossible, for small companies and inventors to enforce patent rights. Several submissions emphasize disproportionate harms to individual inventors and inventor-started companies in post-Alice invalidations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on investment and competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The current state of the law on eligibility has undermined investment in startups, particularly in digital technologies, to such an extent that ‘a number of the large companies [in this space] today face little or no competition.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters linked eligibility uncertainty to reduced formation or growth of startups, difficulties in securing business partnerships, and lost opportunities to advance products—especially in diagnostics and precision medicine—thereby reducing competitive pressure in markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced litigation costs by curbing NPE suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters suggested that the state of the law on eligibility encouraged overly broad patents pre-Alice that gave rise to lawsuits by non-practicing entities (NPEs), and that the current jurisprudence helps curb abusive litigation strategies from NPEs and thus reduces overall legal costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include an estimate of median cost to defend against an NPE suit of $1.7 million and assertions that limiting abstract idea patents reduces nuisance settlements and wasted legal expenditures, allowing startups to deploy capital to R&D instead of defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased costs of obtaining patents (prosecution costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The current jurisprudence significantly increases the costs of obtaining a patent from the USPTO due to protracted cycles of examiner office actions and responses to resolve questions of eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bar associations and practitioners reported substantial increases in prosecution costs, repeated rounds of eligibility rejections, sometimes filing separate applications to carve out more-eligible subject matter, abandonment of applications, and clients electing not to file in the U.S. in affected technologies. Anecdotes include multi-year back-and-forth and large out-of-pocket prosecution expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased post-grant litigation costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of defending a patent once it has been issued has increased as a function of increased frequency of litigation over patent eligibility and new motion practice specific to §101 issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors cited include a reported >141% increase in eligibility-based invalidations in district courts post-Alice, more motions to dismiss/bifurcate/summary judgment on §101 grounds, additional briefing and argument costs, and strategic exploitation of eligibility uncertainty by defendants raising spurious arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased costs for patent counseling and strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of subject matter eligibility has driven up the complexity and cost of patent counseling (including licensing transactions and other patent transactions) and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations report spending more resources developing patent strategies amid uncertainty (e.g., adding foreign outside counsel, increased licensing/transaction costs), detracting from research and product development and increasing overall business legal expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impacts on access to technical information — improved patent disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters asserted that the current jurisprudence has made technical information more readily available and reliable by incentivizing more detailed patent disclosures and marginally narrower claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements include that ‘Alice was a “forcing function”’ leading to more detail in claims and descriptions, resulting in higher-quality patents and better public disclosure that more fully supports the disclosure function of the patent system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impacts on access to technical information — enhanced reliance on trade secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: Frustrated innovators are increasingly turning to trade secrets instead of patent protection, with counsel sometimes advising holding inventions as trade secrets if significant eligibility challenges are anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters warned this shift limits public access to information, injects ‘slowness of discovery’ into industry-wide innovation, may prevent peer review (raising public health/safety concerns), creates indefinite monopolies over information (no expiration), and can steer investment away from ground-breaking therapies.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. global leadership and competitiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The uncertainty and unpredictability in patent eligibility jurisprudence is weakening U.S. leadership in innovation and risks signaling that subject matter once globally accepted as patent eligible can be denied protection in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argued that other countries (e.g., China, EPO jurisdiction) are strengthening patent rights, and that weaker U.S. protections threaten the country’s innovation economy, industrial competitiveness, and ability to secure future, unforeseeable innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: National security implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncertainty in post-Alice §101 jurisprudence poses potential national security risks by undermining U.S. technological leadership in essential and emerging technologies, including AI and telecommunications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders cited the National Security Commission on AI and warned that failing to address eligibility uncertainty could hinder U.S. leadership in foundational technologies, enabling foreign governments and adversaries to control critical technology stacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impacts on life sciences technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The evolving precedent on patent eligibility has had significant impact on life sciences—pharmaceuticals, biologics, medical diagnostics, precision medicine, bioinformatics, and gene-based technologies—because exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena) often implicate these fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life sciences stakeholders stressed high R&D costs (e.g., ~$2.6 billion and ~12 years to bring a medicine to market) and argued that diminished patent protection reduces incentives to make the multi‑million dollar investments required for development and testing, potentially slowing therapeutic advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic innovations — linkage to treatment required
rubrics_metrics.description: Current §101 jurisprudence generally requires that claims to diagnostic tests be linked to affirmative steps reciting methods of treatment; this requirement is counterintuitive because diagnostic companies typically do not provide treatments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters observed that this approach dilutes IP value for diagnostics and implicates divided infringement issues; they also noted that Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., Vanda) recognizing treatment-linked methods have limited practical benefit for diagnostic innovators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences on prosecution behavior and disclosure (narrower claims, abandonment, flight of innovation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The current jurisprudence is resulting in narrower claims; more frequent abandonment of applications; discouragement of disclosure of new innovations; and flight of innovation from the United States to other markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders reported strategic behavior (e.g., filing separate applications to isolate more-eligible subject matter), reduced willingness to disclose inventions, and in some cases opting to seek protection only abroad or rely on non-disclosure to preserve competitive advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secrets’ longer-term market effects (slowness, hoarding, pricing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of trade secrets in lieu of patents can slow discovery across industries, hoard knowledge, and result in higher long-term prices for new products because proprietary ‘know how’ is priced into licenses and tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters warned that unlike patents, trade secrets do not expire, may never become available for public use, can prevent peer review (risking product quality and safety), and elevate costs for downstream users and consumers.
